#5493. Shares of AI cloud operator Nebius drop 16%+ despite strong earnings results

Shares of artificial intelligence cloud operator Nebius Holdings NV dropped 17% today after it posted third-quarter financial results.

The company’s adjusted profit and revenue topped expectations. The selloff may have been sparked by its full-year forecast, which fell short of the consensus estimate. It’s also possible the sudden departure of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Jensen Huang contributed. Nvidia is an investor in Nebius and many other AI and cloud companies.

Another possible factor: Nebius increased its full-year capital spending guidance to $27 billion. According to CNBC, that’s $4.15 billion higher than what Wall Street had expected. The company’s plan to invest between $40 billion and $45 billion in data centers next year surpassed the consensus estimate by an even wider margin.

The surging expenses may be related to its shift away from colocation facilities. Today, about 90% of the company’s infrastructure is located in rented data centers. In contrast, the next 2 gigawatts of computing capacity that it plans to bring online will be mostly powered by internally operated data centers.

“Our focus remains on building a healthy, profitable business for the long term,” said founder and Chief Executive Officer Arkady Volozh. “We will continue to invest across the business – in our capacity and infrastructure buildout, in our platform and products, and in the team that takes this to market.”

Nebius swung from a $100.4 million adjusted loss a year ago to a $90.9 million adjusted profit. The latter figure breaks down to adjusted earnings of 31 cents per share. The company’s profitability surprised analysts, who expected a loss of 69 cents per share.

Revenue growth was another bright spot. Sales jumped 517% year-over-year, to $980.8 million, which put the company well ahead of the $907.5 million consensus estimate.

One of Nebius’ main growth drivers is its Token Factory service for running open-source AI models. Developers use it to host both post-training and inference workloads. Nebius says that the offering, which launched a year ago, is nearing a “multi-hundred-million-dollar run rate” after logging a 17-fold quarter-over-increase in contract value.

Nebius’ largest customers played a particularly important role in its strong quarterly performance. The company signed $12 billion worth of contracts in the three months ended Sept. 30. The haul included multiyear deals with Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and other major tech firms.

The company uses customers’ contract prepayments to finance its data center projects. The company says that the value of the prepayments it received in the third quarter exceeded its capital expenditures. However, the ratio of prepayments to capital expenditures is expected to decline as Nebius ramps up its data center spending. That detail may be yet another factor in today’s stock selloff.

Nebius expects its full-year revenue to be “at the low end” of its $3 billion to $3.4 billion target range. Analysts expected $3.37 billion. For 2027, Nebius is forecasting $12 billion to $13 billion in revenue.

#5492. Las Vegas Is Running Short on $100K-a-Month Rentals as A-Listers and Athletes Drive Demand

While Las Vegas drowns in unsold homes and priced-out buyers sit on the sidelines waiting for lower mortgage rates, the luxury rental sector is booming, fueled by visiting celebrities, professional athletes, and out-of-town millionaires eyeing a permanent move.

In October, Las Vegas’ overall housing inventory reached an all-time high of nearly 11,450 units, up roughly 10% compared to a year ago, as mortgage rates topping 7% left many buyers priced out.

Yet at the very top of the local rental market, the exact opposite is happening.

Local brokers say that demand for rental mansions in Las Vegas and neighboring Henderson, NV, priced between $50,000 to $100,000 per month is severely outstripping supply.

"In the ultraluxury rental space, there's a huge shortage," Natalia Harris, global real estate adviser with Las Vegas Sotheby's International Realty, tells Realtor.com®. There are currently fewer than 10 super-luxury rentals on the market.

"We personally, day to day, feel the frustrations of the shortage of the inventory of these rentals, because we get requests and we can't even keep up with them."

Harris and her husband, fellow Sotheby's adviser Ben Harris, have been actively encouraging developers and investors to create more extravagant rental inventory to keep up with demand.

Alongside celebrity renters, the Harrises often work with out-of-town executives and entrepreneurs who are considering a relocation to Las Vegas but are not sure where exactly to put down roots.

"They're renting for a year maybe, or six months, while they're browsing and shopping for a home and figuring out where they want to be," says Natalia. This class of clients gravitates toward rentals in the $50,000- to $60,000-per-month bracket.

While in the past the biggest feeder market for high-end rentals in Vegas was California, Natalia says over the past year, momentum has shifted to Seattle. Wealthy Washington residents are increasingly eyeing tax-friendly Nevada following the recent passage of the "millionaires tax"—a 9.9% state income tax on earnings exceeding $1 million a year.

Behind this premium rental surge is the valley's rapidly rising cultural cachet.

"Vegas used to be a place where you get a cheap dinner and you gamble, maybe catch a show. But now, Vegas has become the sports and entertainment capital," says Natalia.

In recent years, Las Vegas has cemented its reputation as a top destination for world-class sports, culminating with hosting Super Bowl LVIII in 2024.

The city's jam-packed calendar includes the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix, the NASCAR Cup Series, college football and basketball tournaments, and high-stakes championship boxing. In 2028, Vegas will host the NCAA Men’s Final Four, followed the next year by Super Bowl LXIII.

Beyond headline-making marquee spectacles, Las Vegas has built a thriving local sports scene anchored by championship franchises like the Stanley Cup-winning Vegas Golden Knights and the WNBA champion Las Vegas Aces.

"Vegas has completely evolved, and the attention that we're getting from high net worth individuals ... or celebrities and athletes that are coming here for some of those events, it's just created a whole new dynamic," says Natalia.

Sports is not the city's only draw. As part of the valley's cultural evolution, the Strip has been increasingly attracting A-list entertainers at the peak of their careers, marking a major shift from decades past.

"Vegas used to be a place where artists came when they were toward the end of their career," says Natalia. "Elvis, Frank Sinatra—they would come here as they're winding down for their residencies. Now, that's not the case at all."

The city's most prestigious new venue, the Sphere, has recently featured Backstreet Boys, Metallica, and U2. Pink and John Mayer are slated for upcoming residencies.

"For us in the rental space, that's really where we're seeing our demand, because these artists aren't people that can just walk through the hotel and grab some dinner and be unnoticed and left alone," notes Natalia. "They're going to be swarmed by fans wanting photos, and they need somewhere where they can escape while they're in Vegas."

Affluent clients working with Natalia and her husband often travel with family and aides, and they seek a refuge from the frenzy of the Strip, which they can find in guard-gated golf course communities nestled in the mountains just 15 minutes outside city center.

"A lot of them don't realize there's life off the Strip," says Ben. "Once they find out about that and they stay once, they want to keep coming back."

Demand for luxury rentals in the valley predictably spikes around major events. During the Super Bowl, the Harrises secured accommodations for the families of five top starters from both the San Francisco 49ers and the Kansas City Chiefs.

Summer is a particularly busy season, drawing NBA players to town for the Summer League or off-season workouts at the elite IMPACT Basketball training facility.

These high-profile clients typically rent mansions for one to three months in ultraexclusive enclaves like MacDonald Highlands—a 1,320-acre master-planned golf community nestled in the foothills of the Black and McCullough mountains in Henderson.

The undisputed poster child for this sector of the market is 750 Dragon Ridge Drive in Henderson, which the Harrises rented out for a record-setting $100,000 per month.

The 2.2-acre property features indoor and outdoor basketball courts, a gym, a tennis court, a bowling alley, a spa, and a tour bus hookup that Ben and Natalia had installed at the request of visiting performers. It also includes a separate structure with additional bedrooms and en suite bathrooms to house a celebrity's entourage.

Beyond the square footage and high-end finishes, the most coveted amenity among most big-name Vegas renters is a panoramic view of the glittering Strip.

"Just like if you're going on a beach vacation, you want to make sure your hotel has the oceanfront views, they want to make sure they have that unobstructed Strip view so they can pull out their phone and FaceTime somebody like, 'I told you I'm doing it big in Las Vegas, look at this view of the Strip at night shining.'"

For the Harrises, witnessing their A-list clients take in that view for the first time never gets old.

"It doesn't matter how big the celebrity is, they still get so excited," says Natalia. "And it's so fun to watch that 'awe' moment when they walk into the home and just have the panoramic view of the Las Vegas Strip in front of them. That's our favorite moment."

There are some exceptions, though. Ben shared an anecdote about how, on one occasion, the aides of an unnamed Grammy winner who was staying in town insisted that all the windows be completely blacked out so he could get a good night's rest before his show the following day.

"I'm in there trying to show them the amazing views, and they're like, 'No, we can't see anything but black.' I'm like, 'Oh, just peek out for a second, please!'" he recalls with a laugh.

Once the rental agreement is signed, keeping the world-famous renters happy is the main objective.

"One of the reasons people like to rent through us is because we don't really say no," says Natalia. "If they want something, we make it work. All these homes are definitely dialed in and ready to go, but sometimes people have things that are really special to them."

Typical requests include providing a specific brand of mattress or bed, installing a cold plunge, or reconfiguring the space to create more bedrooms for staff.

Other times, the customization requests are purely for fun, such as painting an NBA team's logo on the basketball court at 750 Dragon Ridge Drive.

"You've got to make it happen at these price points," says Ben. "'No' is not an acceptable answer."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5490. 3 ways AI is changing the healthcare revenue cycle

The healthcare revenue cycle depends on teams investigating denied claims, checking payer rules and deciding which problems need a human’s attention. AI agents could take on some of that work, but the harder question is how to fit them into the way health systems operate.

For Mount Sinai Health System Inc., that starts with clear workflows and accountability when automation encounters an exception, according to Salonia Brown, system vice president of revenue cycle at Mount Sinai. Without those foundations, adding AI could make existing problems harder to manage.

“If you don’t have your workflows down pat, if you don’t have operational owners, when something kicks out, when you use AI, if there’s no ownership over that or accountability, then what you’re in essence doing is kind of digitizing dysfunction,” Brown said in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s very simple and easy to inject AI, but to do it the right way, making sure there’s governance [and] that the economics make sense? That takes a little bit of time.”

Brown and Akash Magoon, co-founder and chief executive officer of Adonis Technology Inc., along with other industry experts, spoke with theCUBE’s host Gemma Allen for the Adonis Reimagining Claim to Cash interview series on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI agents can handle claims work, how health systems govern exceptions and where human judgment remains essential. (* Disclosure below.)

Here are three insights from this exclusive interview series:

Adonis is building agents to investigate denied claims and reduce the manual work involved in pursuing payment, according to Magoon. The company uses voice AI to call insurers for claims information and makes tens of thousands of those calls each week on behalf of its partners.

At Mount Sinai, Brown’s team helps determine which tasks can be automated and which require critical judgment. Employees need to trust the technology and know who is responsible when an exception arises, he noted. The goal is to free staff from repetitive administrative work so they can focus on more complex cases.

Adonis distinguishes between frequent, repetitive tasks suited to automation and complex work that calls for better information and decisions, according to David Unger, managing director of health system sales at Adonis. For a high-value appeal, that can mean helping a team decide whether to pursue it and what evidence may improve its chances.

At Rush University System for Health, frontline employees help identify time-consuming steps that add little value, according to Blake Evans, system vice president of revenue cycle at Rush. Their firsthand knowledge helps the company decide where to automate and has made staff advocates for further changes.

Adonis aims to identify revenue-cycle issues as they emerge and recommend a response, according to Doug Pickett, chief revenue officer of Adonis. An issue might call for automation, or it might reveal an upstream coding or provider-credentialing problem that a health system needs to fix before it grows.

Clinicians and operating teams are increasingly asking for AI tools that could reduce administrative burdens, according to Sap Sinha, chief executive officer of Panoramic Health. Yet rules governing billing, documentation and interactions with insurers have not kept pace with the technology. How those rules evolve could shape whether and how providers and insurers can use AI agents to interact over claims.

#5489. Inside Winter’s Buzziest Getaways—Where Celebrities and Influencers Flock for an Upstate Escape

With cold weather already settling in, A-listers and influencers who call New York City home are heading north to Beacon and the Catskills—turning these upstate towns into the ultimate winter hotspots.

Celebrities and influencers have have been heading over to for an upstate New York escape in winter's hotspots—and their appeal is easy to picture as the cold weather approaches.

Between Beacon’s waterfall-side boutique hotel and the Catskills’ mountain lodges with private soaking tubs, the destinations offer plenty of reasons to leave the city behind for a few days. For some visitors, a weekend away becomes the inspiration for something more permanent.

But what does it cost to buy a place in these coveted retreats, and how much attention are they attracting from New York home shoppers?

The Catskills have drawn Hollywood actors, reality stars, and influencers for vacations, weddings, and a quieter place to call home.

Olivia Wilde and Rami Malek have both stayed at a mountain lodge in Hunter. Jennifer Grey, Ali Wentworth, Olivia Rodrigo, and George Stephanopoulos also headed to the region in 2024 to celebrate the wedding of Schuyler Fox, the daughter of Michael J. Fox and Tracy Pollan.

That same summer, YouTube star Ethan Dolan and influencer Kristina Alice chose the Catskills for their own wedding. Alice later shared photographs from the celebration on Instagram, giving followers a glimpse of their romantic setting.

The fashion crowd has embraced the area, too. Vogue editor Naomi Elizée and Anthony Blue Jr. married in a meadow in Tannersville after welcoming guests for a weekend of festivities.

For Amanda Seyfried, the Catskills offered a place to put down roots. The actress purchased a 1930s farm in 2013 while looking for a retreat from Hollywood, and the property became her main residence.

Across the Hudson, Beacon draws visitors with contemporary art, vintage shops, and an easy trip from New York City. Model and creator Bri Scalesse documented a visit that included Dia Beacon and vintage shopping—an itinerary that works for a day trip or a longer weekend.

According to Realtor.com® data, the median asking price in Beacon was $700,000 in September 2026. In Woodstock, a town included in the Catskills analysis, the median asking price was $968,750 in October.

Those figures offer snapshots of two individual markets. The broader home-search analysis covers all of Dutchess County, where Beacon is located, and five Catskills counties.

According to Realtor.com data, the Catskills accounted for 1.17% of all listing views from the New York City metro in the third quarter of 2026, up from 1.03% a year earlier.

Dutchess County’s share rose from 0.53% to 0.58%, giving the Catskills roughly twice its share of NYC-area browsing.

Both destinations gained a bigger share of a shrinking pool of views. NYC-metro views of Catskills listings fell about 28% year over year, while views of Dutchess County listings declined about 31%. NYC-area views across all listings fell more sharply, by about 37%.

New York remained the largest source of listing views for both destinations, even as shoppers elsewhere accounted for more of their audience. NYC-metro shoppers generated 37.5% of Catskills listing views, down from 42.3% a year earlier. In Dutchess County, their share slipped from 43.3% to 39.8%.

“Winter getaway buzz hasn’t translated into a winter surge in home shopping,” says Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones.

“Interest in the Catskills and Beacon follows normal seasonal patterns, but both places hold on to the attention of New York–area shoppers better than most markets, and they’re taking up a growing share of what those shoppers look at. At the same time, New York–area shoppers make up a smaller share of the audience for each destination than they did a year ago.”

According to Realtor.com data, NYC-metro listing views fell 21% to 25% in the Catskills and 19% to 25% in Dutchess County between the third and fourth quarters over the three years analyzed. Those declines were broadly in line with the national seasonal slowdown.

NYC-area views across all listings fell more sharply, by 30% to 37%, allowing both destinations to capture a larger share of attention heading into the holidays. In 2025, for example, the Catskills’ share of NYC-metro browsing rose from 1.03% in the third quarter to 1.23% in the fourth.

From the fourth quarter to the first, NYC-metro views fell by 2%, 8%, and 15% in the Catskills and by 6%, 5%, and 16% in Dutchess County across the three winters studied. Over those same periods, NYC-metro views across all listings rose by 2% to 10%.

For buyers picturing a winter retreat, the figures show that home browsing in these destinations slows after the holidays, even as New Yorkers’ searches pick up elsewhere.

#5488. Inflation, Supply Policies to Have Most Impact on Housing Affordability Post-Elections: Economists

American voters made it clear that affordability was one of the main drivers that tipped them in favor of putting Democrats in control of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections.

Democratic candidates flipped both the House of Representatives and Senate blue, buoyed by voters who have seen their everyday living costs skyrocket under the second Trump administration—and made it clear they wanted change.

But now the real work of making those campaign promises a reality begins—with housing affordability a top concern. Any solutions Congress might come up with to combat rising housing costs will take time to put into motion and generally inspire bipartisan cooperation, three top economists tell RISMedia.

Before any policies come into play, economists say inflation is a critical risk to mortgage rate stability and, in turn, the health of the housing market.

Inflation, economic headwinds top issues to watch

Getting inflation under control and expanding housing supply without creating outpaced demand could help shape housing affordability, economists say.

October’s hotter-than-expected inflation reading, up 0.4% instead of the 0.3% forecasted month-over-month, makes it highly likely the Federal Reserve will hike rates when it meets in December. In fact, 90% of analysts polled by CME Group anticipate the Fed will hike its target rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4.00% to 4.25%.

“What matters most for buyers and sellers is whether inflation eases and mortgage rates become more affordable and the labor market stays healthy,” says Odeta Kushi, deputy chief economist with First American Financial.

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Another inflationary metric to watch is the U.S. national debt, Kushi notes, which now stands at more than $40 trillion. This will become even more urgent when the current debt limit of $41.1 trillion is reached by May or mid-2027. If there’s a congressional standoff over increasing the debt limit, that could drive inflation—and borrowing costs—higher while creating more financial market volatility, she explained.

But getting inflation under control depends on a lot of moving parts, according to Jake Krimmel, senior economist with Realtor.com®. Under the Trump administration, it’s impossible to pinpoint those moving parts amid a trade war (and tariffs), geopolitical tensions and mixed economic readings.

Krimmel stressed that inflation also erodes purchasing power. “Inflation eats away at paychecks and makes it harder for people to save.”

“The big wild card heading into 2027 is the same one that we’ve been talking about probably since February, which is the effect of the (Iran) War on the longer end of the curve, the Fed’s rate path and the economy more broadly, especially with respect to inflation, consumer confidence and consumer spending,” Krimmel says. “We don’t know what 2027 will bring, but uncertainty is a feature in this market.”

Mischa Fisher, Zillow’s chief economist, points to a simple formula that will bring mortgage rates down to more palatable levels for homebuyers to act.

“We know, generally speaking, that the best way out of this is higher incomes, lower mortgage rates and more supply,” Fisher says.

According to Zillow’s October housing report, the monthly mortgage payment on the typical U.S. home reached $2,004, up 12.8% from a year ago. That means a median-income household would need to spend 34.7% of its income on total housing costs—up from 32.7% a year ago and far beyond the typical 30% benchmark, Zillow reported.

Fisher noted that the Democrats’ sweep of the midterms hasn’t altered Zillow’s housing forecasts, which call for rates to stay in the 7% range, flat-to-lower sales volume compared to 2026 and home values that rise slightly on paper but decline slightly in real terms after adjusting for inflation.

Could Congress pull any meaningful levers for housing?

When the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, they’ll have their work cut out for them to deliver for voters who made affordability a central election motivation. However, with President Donald Trump already pledging to use the power of his pen to veto Democrat-led bills, will any meaningful housing legislation see the light of day?

“When we have this period where Congress is controlled by one party and the executive branch is controlled by the other party, typically, that doesn’t foretell close collaboration on policy,” Fisher says. “But I think we have seen that in the case of housing, there is a bipartisan agreement that there’s room to improve the environment. That’s what we’re watching to see play out.”

Fisher notes that the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed earlier this year, offers “a real bipartisan blueprint for how policymakers can work together to specifically improve housing.” The timing couldn’t be more crucial as the gap between Americans’ incomes and affordable housing widens.

Kushi adds that Congress should look at policies that make it “easier, cheaper and faster to build and bring more homes to the market.”

While it’s too early to know what lawmakers have in mind to help ease affordability pressures in the housing market, Krimmel cautions that any government stalemates—a shutdown or lapses in government funding—could be disastrous for the 10-year Treasury yield, which directly impacts mortgage rate movements. A government shutdown can also disrupt economic data collection, making it harder to gauge progress on inflation.

“We already have enough pressure on the 10-year,” Krimmel says. “We don’t need anything else.”

All three economists agree that improving housing affordability involves addressing the supply side, among other action items.

The U.S. has an estimated supply gap of 4.03 million homes, according to Realtor.com. Closing the gap, Krimmel says, means boosting new construction, which needs to be “easier to build.” Lawmakers should “encourage states and localities to adopt more permissive local zoning laws and also streamline that permitting process,” Krimmel says, cautioning that it will take time to see any gains.

For now, Realtors® should track local inventory and price trends to help guide their clients more effectively. Fisher notes that affordability-related softness and price pressures will persist in parts of the Mountain West and Sun Belt, while supply-constrained coastal markets where new building isn’t as robust face upward pressure.

Existing-home inventory is still being suppressed by the mortgage lock-in effect, as owners may be reluctant to sell and give up their pandemic-era low rates. More realistic pricing from sellers can help listings go under contract and give buyers more negotiating power. But a more buyer-friendly market doesn’t necessarily mean homes are affordable to more buyers, Krimmel says.

Only time will tell if income growth can keep up with housing costs—and if Congress can act quickly enough to start meaningfully improving affordability to help ease Americans’ financial strain.

Deborah Kearns is a freelance editor and writer with more than 15 years of experience covering real estate, mortgages and personal finance topics. Her work has appeared in The New York Times, Forbes Advisor, The Associated Press, MarketWatch, USA Today, MSN and HuffPost, among others. Deborah previously held editorial leadership and writing roles at NerdWallet, Bankrate, LendingTree and RE/MAX World Headquarters.

#5487. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

Here’s the usual scenario: You sign up for a coaching program. You’re excited, and you should be. Everybody wants to feel a little less alone in a job you mostly do by yourself, in your car.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

The reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

What would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

#5486. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. #5485. What to expect during SC26: Join theCUBE Nov. 17–19

High-performance computing and artificial intelligence are converging, driven by advances in exascale computing, accelerated systems, data storage and high-speed networking.

The convergence of these technologies is a prime topic for discussion during SC26 in Chicago this month. Major industry players, such as Dell Technologies Inc., Google LLC and Nvidia Corp., have pursued a set of initiatives in the HPC arena, and SC26 will be an occasion to learn more about how AI and HPC workloads are evolving to write supercomputing’s next chapter.

“SC26 provides an important opportunity to examine how the convergence of AI, high-performance computing and application development are reshaping enterprise infrastructure priorities,” said theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty. “Organizations must connect high-performance infrastructure, accessible data and modern application development to move beyond experimentation and accelerate production-ready AI deployments. For Dell and the broader HPC ecosystem, SC26 offers a platform to demonstrate how integrated compute, storage and AI infrastructure can address these challenges.”

TheCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, will be covering the latest HPC news and announcements from SC26 in Chicago, Nov. 17–19. Coverage will feature on-site reporting and exclusive interviews with industry leaders and analysts as theCUBE explores how supercomputing’s future is being shaped at the intersection of exascale systems and AI infrastructure. Discussion will focus on ways that accelerated computing is transforming research environments, while quantum-HPC integration and agentic AI push scientific discovery toward greater autonomy. (* Disclosure below.)

Dell’s ongoing collaboration with Nvidia and other organizations has yielded several new developments in the HPC arena over the past year, particularly in the area of quantum computing.

The two companies have been working with the U.S. Department of Energy to build and deliver the Doudna supercomputer at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The system will use Nvidia’s Vera Rubin CPU-GPU platform and Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking inside Dell’s integrated rack systems and PowerEdge servers to support large-scale scientific computing and data-intensive research.

In September, Dell announced a collaboration with silicon-spin qubit developer Diraq to integrate quantum processing units with HPC and AI server infrastructure. The joint effort is designed to integrate quantum processors with classical computing infrastructure in commercial data centers.

Moves such as these point toward a convergence of AI and quantum technologies, which will likely propel both forward as new platforms are built and deployed.

“The market for high-performance computing is meeting the AI factory at the point of innovation,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante. “HPC has always led the most challenging data problems, so this trend makes perfect sense. Quantum will be the next big inflection point and we’re seeing that new technologies are often complementary to existing infrastructure. We expect that to be the case between accelerated computing and quantum, particularly in the area of error correction.”

Hyperscaler Google Cloud is also building systems to support HPC demands for industries like manufacturing, health care and life sciences, weather forecasting and electronic design automation.

At the forefront of Google’s HPC initiative is the H4D VM, the company’s high-performance computing virtual machine. Introduced last year, the H4D VM is powered by fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors and offers whole-node VM performance of more than 12,000 GFLOPS and memory bandwidth exceeding 950 GB/s.

An example of how HPC is making inroads in daily life can be seen in the use of H4D VMs by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. In July, Google Cloud announced that it had been selected as the primary provider of high-performance computing infrastructure for the Weather and Climate Operational Supercomputing System.

The adoption of HPC to enable meteorologists and researchers to develop future forecasting models is an example of how systems technology will play a critical role in both supercomputing and AI infrastructure moving forward.

“Systems are the key in supercomputing advances,” said theCUBE Research’s John Furrier. “Different architectures. Different bets. Same underlying problem: How do you keep the multiplication engines doing useful work instead of waiting for data? That’s why I think the next era of AI infrastructure won’t be defined by the ‘best chip.’ It will be defined by the best system architecture.”

While the field of HPC is being defined by major players such as Dell and Google, other firms are making contributions as well in areas such as cloud infrastructure and analytics.

Vultr Inc. is building high-performance cloud computing infrastructure for AI, risk management, compliance and fraud prevention. The company is developing its platform across 33 global regions by leveraging CPUs, GPUs and open, composable architectures to position itself as a cloud infrastructure specialist in the agentic AI era.

High-performance computing is also generating a need for consistent data sharing and access across platforms. Omni Analytics Inc. is building a data collaboration solution that can connect directly to cloud data warehouses without needing to preload or duplicate data.

SC26 will offer an opportunity to not only assess the progress of HPC in the enterprise but also examine how AI is continuing to transform the compute stack to generate meaningful business results.

“As organizations invest in increasingly sophisticated AI environments, the competitive differentiator will be the ability to optimize the entire technology stack from data movement and storage performance to application development and deployment,” Nashawaty said. “The central SC26 narrative is that the future of AI supercomputing will be defined not simply by how much compute organizations deploy, but by how effectively they translate that investment into measurable business and scientific outcomes.”

Don’t miss theCUBE’s coverage of SC26, Nov. 17–19. Plus, you can access theCUBE’s exclusive content on demand after the event.

We offer various ways for you to watch theCUBE’s coverage of SC26, including theCUBE’s dedicated website and YouTube channel. You can also get all the coverage from this year’s events on SiliconANGLE.

SiliconANGLE’s “theCUBE Pod” is available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube, which you can enjoy while on the go. During each podcast, SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante discuss the biggest trends in enterprise tech, including AI, cloud, cybersecurity and infrastructure, with context and analysis.

SiliconANGLE also produces our weekly “Breaking Analysis” program, where Vellante examines major developments in enterprise tech, combining insights from theCUBE with spending data from Enterprise Technology Research, available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube.

At SC26, theCUBE will speak with tech leaders and industry analysts about ways that accelerated computing is transforming research environments, while quantum-HPC integration and agentic AI push scientific discovery toward greater autonomy.

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for SC26. Sponsors of theCUBE’s event coverage do not have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)

Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. Join theCUBE’s Alumni Trust Network, where technology leaders connect, share intelligence and create opportunities.

Founded by tech visionaries John Furrier and Dave Vellante, SiliconANGLE Media has built a dynamic ecosystem of industry-leading digital media brands that reach 15+ million elite tech professionals. Our new proprietary theCUBE AI Video Cloud is breaking ground in audience interaction, leveraging theCUBEai.com neural network to help technology companies make data-driven decisions and stay at the forefront of industry conversations.

#5484. Inside a Secluded $3.3 Million Mediterranean Estate With a Resort-Inspired Backyard Retreat in Agoura Hills

An ultra-private estate in Agoura Hills, CA has hit the market, offering a secluded retreat in the Santa Monica Mountains for $3.295 million.

"It's tucked away into the hills and no one's around you. It's just a super private property," listing agent Michelle Meyers of The Agency tells Realtor.com®.

Set on an expansive lot that's just over an acre in the exclusive Heritage View Estates enclave, Meyers notes it's rare to find a home in the area with a yard that's this sizable and this private.

The five-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom abode spans 4,161 square feet—boasting open spaces that are defined by soaring ceilings and 10-inch-wide plank oak floors.

"It's been tailored for such effortless living," Meyers continues, noting that the sellers thoughtfully curated the 1996-built home to maximize every inch of the property, such as perfectly-organized closets in the primary suite and a "completely-custom built out" pantry in the kitchen.

Of the thoughtful upgrades, the beautifully-remodeled kitchen is surely a standout, where timeless design has been leveled-up with top-of-the-line appliances, stunning countertops, and designer lighting.

The ground floor is an excellent spot to entertain from the moment visitors step through the grand entry, which features custom doors and a statement-making curved staircase.

A stately great room has been intentionally arranged to upgrade everyday life, with sliding glass doors providing access to the picturesque exterior space, a modern marble fireplace, and a funky bar.

The main level also includes a "chic powder room," and a private en-suite bedroom that could be well-suited to serve as a home office or a welcoming space for guests.

The remainder of the bedrooms are upstairs, including the lavish, light-flooded primary suite. The room feels like a true escape, thanks to its expansive wraparound balcony, sizable walk-in closet, and spa-inspired bathroom with an oversized shower and relaxing soaking tub.

While this property conveniently provides easy-access to everything a busy family could need, it's also the kind of place they'll want to spend as much time as possible enjoying.

The tranquil outdoor space is truly a vacation-like getaway, primed for relaxation and entertaining alike.

The lush greenery can be enjoyed from the large oversized outdoor living area. The impressive pool is certainly the trophy of the backyard, and features a spacious spa, accessible by a pair of stone steps.

A separate pool house is exceptionally versatile, with a gorgeous bathroom and space that can be utilized by guests or the residents who may want to dedicate additional room to poolside living.

There's also a four-car garage complete with custom epoxy flooring. Functional luxuries include a whole-house water filtration system, smart home technology, and solar panels that have already been fully paid-off.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5483. Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

Can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s new monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

“Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

The time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Debt was a big part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and said the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on new real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and new ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb plans to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the company said in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment issues, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

“Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”

The announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the company’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first announced in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

“Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner said in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”

For agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

#5482. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

#5481. As AI agents take control, Nvidia rethinks the security playbook

Nvidia Corp. recently added a new pillar to its AI networking infrastructure with the unveiling of Scale-In.

Scale-In brings purpose-built acceleration to secure, manage and operate agentic AI factories. It is designed to deliver secure access, high-performance data movement, tenant isolation, simpler operations and more predictable performance as agents assume increasingly larger roles within AI factories.

“In agentic AI, it’s a completely different use case because now we’re dealing with many agents that need to run on the infrastructure,” said Gilad Shainer (pictured), senior vice president of networking at Nvidia. “You need to increase security because you need to make sure that those agents are contained in their sandbox and are not doing the wrong things. You need to build an infrastructure that needs to ensure security all around…what happens in the memory, what happens on storage. This is why we needed to bring an infrastructure which actually enabled the security across everything. And that’s what Scale-In is.”

Shainer spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante for theCUBE + NYSE Wired: AI Factories – Data Centers of the Future interview series on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Nvidia’s Scale-In architecture is designed to help transform scaled compute into a secure and operational AI factory platform.

Since the August introduction, Nvidia has expanded its agent security strategy. In September, the company introduced its Open Agent Safety Platform, combining OpenShell with Nvidia Sentry for out-of-band monitoring and hardware-based security enforcement. An October announcement added the OpenShell Reference Architecture, integrating Vera Rubin infrastructure, Vera CPUs and BlueField-4 to support secure agent execution across enterprise systems. Nvidia’s announcement outlines the expanded architecture.

Scale-In is powered by Nvidia BlueField-4 and Nvidia DOCA and connected over Nvidia Spectrum-X Ethernet. BlueField-4 is Nvidia’s fourth-generation data processing unit, a networking platform built for agentic AI factories and large-scale infrastructure needs. BlueField is essential to the management of agentic AI security, according to Shainer.

“You can think about BlueField or Blue-Field-4 as a device that has in-silicon security engines that are working out of band and collecting telemetry from everything, from memory, from storage, from GPUs, from CPUs,” Shainer told theCUBE. “That’s why that infrastructure connects to all other infrastructures and ensures security all around. That out-of-band monitoring enables BlueField to actually understand exactly what agents are doing.”

Along with BlueField-4, Nvidia DOCA also powers Scale-In deployment. This software platform enables the rapid creation of apps and services that offload, accelerate and isolate data center workloads.

Using DOCA, developers can create software-defined, cloud-native, DPU- and SuperNIC-accelerated solutions. Like Nvidia CUDA, which provides a programming platform for GPU workloads, DOCA gives developers access to DPU acceleration capabilities.

“DPU brings the in-silicon engines security engines, storage accelerations,” Shainer explained. “DOCA is the framework, the software, the APIs that enable you to access all of those engines that BlueField-4 provides.”

Nvidia has further reinforced agentic AI security with its open-source runtime offering called OpenShell. The tool is designed to govern agent execution, access and inference routing. Nvidia combined OpenShell with BlueField-4 because it wanted a device that could collect information outside the GPU and monitor an environment that no agent could influence.

“I want to also have another device which is completely separated, completely isolated from the agents, that can monitor everything out-of-band,” Shainer said. “That’s what we’re doing with BlueField-4, bringing all the security elements together with OpenShell, and now you have a secure infrastructure for agents. This is how the combination of OpenShell and BlueField-4 brings all the security elements that we need for gen AI.”

The more recent OpenShell Reference Architecture builds on that approach with Nvidia Sentry, which runs on BlueField-4 using DOCA software. According to Nvidia, Sentry continuously monitors agent behavior and can quarantine agents that attempt to move outside their defined software boundaries. The combination extends OpenShell’s runtime controls with an independent enforcement layer.

#5480. Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

“Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant said in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”

Yun and Sturtevant said mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant said. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

As a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

“Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he said. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

“If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

“Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she said. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”

Hale said jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

“[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she said. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”

Yun said rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

“One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he said. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the big change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”

However, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on new pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”
