#5460. Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson said in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it said already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the company.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson said.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter said.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The new complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

On Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

On Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the issue in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the company’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS announced plans for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton said the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

The growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

Compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

#5459. Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to plan. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

Not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

What I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a new closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

There’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5458. Cisco beats expectations, lifts guidance and forecasts AI infrastructure revenue to double in fiscal 2027

Shares of Cisco Systems Inc. were flat in late trading today after the networking infrastructure giant reported first-quarter earnings and revenue that came in ahead of Wall Street’s expectations.

The company also raised its guidance for fiscal 2027, citing strong demand for artificial intelligence network infrastructure.

Cisco reported earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $1.40 per share, comfortably beating the Street’s target of $1.33 per share. Revenue for the quarter jumped 24% from the same period one year earlier, to $18.5 billion, ahead of the $18.1 billion analyst consensus estimate. All told, Cisco’s net income rose to $4.6 billion, up from just $2.9 billion a year ago.

Although the stock was flat in extended trading, it’s still up 32% in the year to date, way ahead of the broader Nasdaq index, which has gained just 9% over the same stretch.

Cisco has been pushing to gain a foothold in the AI infrastructure buildout that’s dominating the technology industry these days after failing to capitalize on the generative AI boom in the early days. However, its push has come at a critical juncture, as investors have become increasingly concerned over the prospects of a slowdown in data center building following the Democratic party’s sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections. Additionally, there are growing fears about the impact rising borrowing costs will have on debt-fueled data center construction projects.

Still, Cisco Chief Executive Chuck Robbins (pictured) expressed confidence in the company’s ability to maintain its momentum. He told analysts on a conference call that we’re still in the “very early stages of a multiyear network supercycle.” He said he’s confident Cisco’s AI networking technology is strong enough to continue to capture a portion of the multibillion-dollar opportunity that presents.

“Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era,” Robbins added.

Cisco is also building out its software portfolio with new tools that can help businesses to build armies of autonomous AI agents that can perform work on behalf of humans. It also sells the security software necessary to protect those agents and their underlying infrastructure against cyberattacks.

The company said it’s increasing its AI infrastructure revenue forecast for the fiscal year to $9 billion, which would be more than double what it earned in fiscal 2026. According to Chief Financial Officer Mark Patterson, the company is “unlocking significant operating leverage,” and this is what’s enabling it to grow its earnings “much faster” than its revenue.

Investors may still be worried about Cisco’s gross margins, though. This has been a concern for many companies, as the global shortage of memory chips has steadily increased the cost of the components that hardware makers need to build their data center infrastructure products.  Cisco’s gross margin of 65.6% in the quarter was in-line with the Street’s estimates, but down from 68.1% in the year-ago period.

TECHnalysis Research analyst Bob O’Donnell told Reuters that the decline was unlikely to worry too many people, though. “A small dip in gross margin is not a major concern given higher memory and component costs,” he said. He added that the company’s raised forecast and strong earnings and revenue was the main thing the market wanted to see.

If there is still a concern for investors, it’s most likely the fact that virtually all of Cisco’s growth comes from its core networking business, rather than “growth” bets such as security, observability and collaboration, said Holger Mueller of Constellation Research. “Cisco did really well, with revenue growing 24% and income up 59%, but this was primarily all driven by network demand, which calls into question its other bets. But the good news is that the need for AI networks remains very strong and is growing, and that means good times are ahead for Cisco and its backers.”

For the current quarter, Cisco said it’s looking for earnings of between $1.34 and $1.36 per share on sales of $18 billion to $18.2 billion. That’s a strong forecast, with the Street looking for earnings of just $1.23 per share on revenue of $17.88 billion.

#5457. Applied Materials posts impressive 53% jump in revenue as it beats expectations again

Semiconductor industry giant Applied Materials Inc. chalked up another strong quarter as it continued to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom, delivering fourth-quarter results that surpassed Wall Street’s expectations on earnings and revenue.

The company reported adjusted earnings of $4.16 per share on revenue of $10.41 billion, up by an impressive 53% from a year earlier. The results were impressive, with analysts modeling earnings of just $4.06 per share on sales of $10.3 billion. Net income rose to $2.71 billion, up from $1.89 billion in the same period one year ago.

Applied Materials is the world’s biggest supplier of the equipment used by semiconductor manufacturers such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. and Micron Technology Inc., so its results are widely seen as a bellwether for the broader chipmaking industry. If Applied is growing, it means chipmakers are investing in their factories and presumably expecting to churn out more chips, driving growth in the industry. The company manufactures all sorts of machines to support different semiconductor manufacturing processes, catering to the most advanced silicon for AI workloads.

Chief Executive Gary Dickerson (pictured) said the company delivered record-breaking results in fiscal 2026, with full-year sales rising 21% from the prior year, to $34.31 billion. He also said the semiconductor systems business unit is on track to grow more than 40% in calendar 2026. “AI continues to fuel strong incremental demand for semiconductors and Applied has the most-enabling portfolio to advance the AI computing roadmap, putting us in a great position for multiyear revenue and profit growth,” he added.

Applied’s stock was under pressure earlier in the day following the news of Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, which came after he admitted to having an affair with a woman who is believed to be working for China’s intelligence services. Some investors worry that instability at Nvidia, which is the world’s most dominant AI chip supplier, could have a knock-on effect on the broader chipmaking industry.

However, the strong results brought Applied’s daytime slide to a halt, and the stock gained more than 2.5% in late trading. In the year to date, its stock is up 48%.

Applied’s main business, the semiconductor systems unit, saw revenue jump from $4.88 billion in the year-ago period to $7.99 billion. Meanwhile, sales from the smaller applied global services segment rose from $1.5 billion a year earlier, to $1.89 billion.

Constellation Research analyst Holger Mueller said Applied Material’s ongoing success is due to its unique position in the chip industry, which allows it to benefit from the growing sales of AI chips and also the surging demand for the memory hardware that accompanies those chips. “Gary Dickerson and his team are managing this growth extremely well,” the analyst said. “Last year the company earned $1 from every $4 it generated in revenue, and that is now up to $1 for every $3.50 in sales. Unless the AI boom suddenly collapses, the future for Applied looks extremely bright.”

For the current quarter, Applied said it’s looking for earnings of $4.35 per share at the midpoint of its guidance range, with revenue coming to $11.1 billion. Those numbers were better than expected too, with the Street modeling first quarter earnings of just $4.24 per share on sales of $10.85 billion.

During the quarter, Applied made a big splash when it said it’s going to invest $5 billion in a new chip research and development facility located in Silicon Valley. It’s called the EPIC Center, and it will act as a shared R&D center for chipmakers to collaborate on new process manufacturing technologies.

Initial partners include Intel Corp., which is working with Applied and other companies on the development of next-generation transistors, interconnects and advanced packaging technologies. Other founding partners include Kioxia Corp., BE Semiconductor Industries N.V. and the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering.

#5455. Bitcoin Price Rebounds Despite Quantum Threat as Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Faces Ouster After Two Affairs

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price has rebounded from recent lows as Nvidia board considers ousting CEO Jensen Huang following revelations about two extramarital affairs. Meanwhile, Glassnode data shows that 7.12 million BTC, worth more than $500 billion, already has publicly visible keys that future quantum computers could potentially exploit.

The developments put two of the technology industry’s biggest names under pressure. Bitcoin faces growing questions about its long-term cryptographic security, while Nvidia confronts a leadership crisis that could draw its AI dominance and ambitions in quantum computing.

Nvidia shares plunged more than 8% in extended trading after reports emerged that directors were preparing to remove Huang. The board is also considering an interim CEO before launching a wider search for a permanent replacement.

Bitcoin price recovered from its November 10 low of $72,600, reaching around $74,000 before easing to $73,700 this morning. The rebound offers bulls some relief after a sharp correction earlier this month. However, Glassnode has identified a potentially huge vulnerability affecting more than a third of Bitcoin’s issued supply.

According to a Glassnode update, approximately 35.4% of Bitcoin’s supply, equivalent to 7.12 million BTC, has publicly visible keys. At current market prices, those holdings are valued at more than $500 billion.

The exposure largely comes from address reuse. When Bitcoin holders spend from an address, their public keys become visible on the blockchain. Any remaining coins associated with those keys could become targets for sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Glassnode also says moving those coins to fresh addresses ends this exposure.

The concern centers on Shor’s algorithm, which could theoretically allow quantum computers to derive private keys from publicly available information. That would undermine the cryptographic security protecting vulnerable Bitcoin holdings.

Bitcoin developers are already exploring ways to address the challenge. BIP 360 proposes new transaction structures designed to reduce public-key exposure, while BIP 361 outlines a potential migration away from vulnerable signature schemes.

Nvidia’s leadership crisis has escalated dramatically after Reuters reported that its board was meeting late Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang. The 63-year-old founder has led Nvidia for more than three decades, transforming it into the dominant supplier of AI processors. But revelations about two extramarital relationships have triggered an internal investigation and intensified scrutiny of his leadership.

The first controversy involves Alice Huang, a businesswoman whose relationship with Jensen Huang has attracted attention from US intelligence officials. She is reportedly suspected of facilitating Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies. The investigation has raised concerns about potential Chinese intelligence involvement and whether Nvidia’s technology reached restricted customers.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, is now working with an "outside firm" to find a new CEO to replace Jensen Huang, per Bloomberg.The company is also reportedly weighing naming a temporary CEO while searching for a replacement.

A second relationship emerged through a New York Times report identifying Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Powell reportedly worked directly under Huang, creating additional corporate governance questions.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees, taking responsibility for his actions. The board’s response has shifted rapidly. Directors previously expressed confidence in Huang, but Bloomberg subsequently reported that Nvidia had engaged an outside firm to identify potential replacements.

It should be noted that Nvidia has 11 directors, with all but Huang considered independent. Its bylaws allow a majority vote to remove the CEO.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has emerged as a potential interim successor, while data-center executive Ian Buck has attracted attention as a possible longer-term candidate. The timing is particularly sensitive, with Nvidia scheduled to release quarterly results on November 17.

Bitcoin’s market recovery remains an important counterpoint for all these developments. Bitcoin price has managed to recover from its November 10 sell-off, with buyers stepping in around $72,700. Reclaiming $74,000 would give bulls another opportunity to challenge higher resistance levels.

The quantum threat is pushing developers to consider changes that could strengthen Bitcoin’s security over the coming years. Nvidia faces a different challenge. Losing Huang would remove the founder most closely associated with its AI dominance, potentially forcing investors to reassess the company’s leadership and long-term strategy.

The $500 billion quantum exposure has added another major scare to the market. But Bitcoin’s ability to adapt could become just as important as its price performance.

#5454. Five thoughts from Cisco’s first quarter of fiscal 2027

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Cisco Systems Inc. opened fiscal 2027 with a quarter that should put any question about whether artificial intelligence will act as a massive tailwind for it to rest. Revenue and earnings hit records, growth rates were the best Cisco has posted in more than 15 years, and management raised its full-year outlook and AI infrastructure revenue target.

While Cisco has delivered a string of solid quarters, some investors are concerned about the durability of the growth. After listening to the analyst call, I maintain that accelerated growth is what Cisco watchers should expect, as AI will act as a catalyst for several years. Here are my five thoughts, plus the one metric I think investors should care about most:

Asked why this isn’t simply the top of a hyperscaler spending cycle, Chief Executive Chuck Robbins (pictured) cited five growth drivers: hyperscale AI, the campus refresh, the “post-Mythos” security upgrade cycle, sovereign infrastructure and enterprise hybrid data centers. “All five of these are multiyear, multibillion,” he said. “And they’re all in relatively early stages.” In particular, the enterprise opportunity is in its infancy. Using the baseball analogy for “what inning” we’re in, the pitchers are still warming up, and enterprise is what Cisco does best.

Though hyperscalers have been driving AI growth across the industry, only one of the five trends Robbins highlighted was related to that group of companies. Chief Financial Officer Mark Patterson reinforced the point by breaking down the guidance raise, noting that a large share came from Cisco’s core, non-hyperscale business. “It’s not just campus,” he said. “It’s broad-based, and the core continues to do quite well.”

The market still views the enterprise as a slow-refresh business. The call made a strong case that it’s about to become the bigger part of Cisco’s AI story.

During the investor Q&A, a data point was worth highlighting. Robbins said that of the campus switching Cisco sold this quarter, “only 9% was really coming from the new portfolio.” Despite multiple quarters of strong campus growth, the installed base has barely moved to the next generation.

Two forces will push this base to accelerate an upgrade. One is agentic AI, which Robbins said is driving “modernization for bandwidth reasons” because agents generate traffic that campus networks were never designed to handle. The other is the security fallout from frontier models such as Anthropic’s Claude Mythos — the Mythos moment. “We’re beginning to hear from customers who are attributing orders to early Mythos implications,” Robbins said, noting that European service providers are upgrading managed customer premises equipment.

Robbins added that customers “got to get the architecture exactly right.” That suggests a long, deliberate redesign rather than a buying spree, which is characteristic of a multiyear cycle.

Cisco has long been criticized for building its own silicon as the industry shifted to merchant silicon. Robbins said that outside of optics, the hyperscale AI business is “100% Silicon One-based platforms.” The P200 continues to win scale-across deals, and the G300 is now in customer labs.

Asked why Cisco keeps winning those deals, Robbins kept it simple: “It’s really about performance and power. And there’s just this whole focus on diversity of silicon in the space.” The second point is the more strategic one. No hyperscaler wants a single supplier for any critical layer of its AI fabric, and Cisco is the credible second source.

The bigger long-term play is the enterprise. Silicon One is already shipping across parts of the enterprise portfolio, and Robbins said the target to convert all of it by fiscal 2029 “is still on track.” That gives Cisco a single silicon architecture from the hyperscale data center to the branch, with cost and roadmap control competitors can’t match.

The reality is that at Cisco’s volumes, it makes no sense to buy merchant silicon. Not only can it build it cheaper, but it can also optimize it specifically for its own features and capabilities.

A theme running through the call is that AI is decentralizing. “Our enterprise customers will be running AI applications in the cloud, but they’re also investing heavily in private data centers,” Robbins said. “They want to run open-weight and open-source models in their own data centers. They want to train on their own data in their own data centers.”

Sovereignty is driving in the same direction, with Cisco extending its Sovereign Critical Infrastructure portfolio from Europe to Canada and preannouncing India. Robbins noted that Cisco is “one of the few companies that has maintained a robust on-premises portfolio.” For years, analysts treated that on-premises focus as a liability. In a world where countries and regulated industries want operational control, it has become an advantage.

Equally important is what Cisco isn’t chasing. Robbins called neocloud exposure “relatively immaterial,” adding that “we’ve been very conservative relative to the credit situations.” That’s a disciplined choice. Cisco is growing into the safest parts of the AI build-out rather than financing its riskiest buyers.

Given the number of neoclouds, one could look at them as a massive pot of gold, but they often required vendor financing. If the neocloud isn’t successful, it’s the financing organization left holding the bag. This was the case with CLECs in the Internet days. Cisco was conservative then and will continue to be.

Security has been the weak spot in Cisco’s story, so this quarter’s progress matters. Robbins said core security orders, excluding Splunk, were “the best it’s been in three years,” with firewalls, Zero Trust secure access, and AI Defense all gaining customers. Patterson said Cisco is “a little bit above the expectations that we set out” and feels “good about turning the corner.”

The refresh cycle drives near-term numbers, but the strategic prize is trust for AI agents. Robbins said enterprise conversations now center on “agentic security, agentic identity, agentic observability, as well as the new security architecture needed for the AI era.” The network is where agent traffic flows, making it the natural enforcement point. Cisco owns more of that network than anyone.

Investor concerns received clear answers. On margins, Patterson said, “gross margins are pretty much right on target,” and on supply, “we’re seeing not a lot of issues at all.” Robbins added that Cisco is growing revenue “with less headcount than we had at the beginning” two years ago.

The number I’d watch most closely isn’t AI revenue, campus orders, or gross margin. It’s the growth of Cisco Cloud Control. Robbins mentioned it almost in passing, noting thousands of sign-ups and integrations with AI Canvas, Cisco IQ and Cisco Model Foundry. Most people will think of Cloud Control as a network management tool, but that badly understates its potential.

Cloud Control is now Cisco’s core product. The best analogy is VMware vCenter, the data center’s control point that turned a collection of products into a sticky platform. Cheaper, sometimes free hypervisors never made a dent in VMware’s share because the operational control gained from vCenter far outweighed the few bucks saved on hypervisor licenses. Cloud Control is broader and potentially more impactful because Cisco is positioning it as the control point for enterprise AI, not just the network through the following capabilities.

Cisco’s numerous network and security competitors have their own agentic operations platforms, and many beat Cisco to market. However, Cisco played the long game. In my conversations with Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel, he has been emphatic about how important Cloud Control is to Cisco’s vision of shifting to a platform company. It enables customers to manage the underlying infrastructure, including third parties, through a single dashboard.

If Cloud Control becomes the enterprise IT console for managing AI-era infrastructure, Cisco stops competing on boxes and starts competing on control. Hardware cycles always ebb and flow, so always being best of breed is impossible. Whether this one becomes a transformation for Cisco depends on whether customers run their environments on Cloud Control. My advice to Cisco is to start disclosing active usage, partner integrations, and attach rates for the platform.

My advice to investors is to start asking for them. That number will tell you what Cisco is worth five years from now.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5453. A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he said.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively new sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

What you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he said.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

And when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré said; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

#5450. Google Cloud takes aim at the cost of keeping idle AI agents running on Kubernetes

Kubernetes has become the go-to platform for distributed training and inference, but what happens to the compute bill when it runs AI agents that spend most of their time waiting?

When an agent’s container or virtual machine stays provisioned, customers pay for the wait as well as the work. To help customers control those costs and make agent workloads more predictable, Google LLC has donated three projects to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, according to Allan Naim (pictured, left), director of product management, AI infrastructure, at Google Cloud. For Kubernetes itself, the new challenge is freeing up compute between bursts of activity while letting each agent pick up where it left off.

“Act 2 is a few years back; Kubernetes became the de facto for inference and training,” Naim said. “What’s really interesting right now is we’re embarking on this Act 3 … where the typical patterns are very, very different from how Kubernetes was designed.”

Naim and Gari Singh (right), product manager at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Google Cloud is using open-source tools to cut compute costs when AI agents sit idle. (* Disclosure below.)

Cost presents a serious problem in agentic workloads, with agents sitting idle 90% to 95% of the time waiting on models, test runs or human approvals, Naim explained. Google developed Agent Substrate, an open-source runtime that hosts AI agents in isolated environments on Kubernetes. When an agent is suspended, the runtime saves a snapshot of its memory and local files and frees up its compute for other agents. When work resumes, it restores the agent from that snapshot in an available sandbox.

“It helps from an economic standpoint,” Naim said. “We’ve seen 10x reduction in cost in terms of running Agent Substrate on Kubernetes versus running these agents directly on dedicated virtual machines and containers.”

Security is another concern. In response, Google open-sourced gVisor in 2018, which sits on top of the host kernel to block or audit every system call an agent makes, according to Singh.

“Agents and agent harnesses are designed to solve a problem — and to try to solve a problem — until they can’t solve the problem,” Singh said. “They will find all kinds of clever workarounds. They know everything that’s around. You want to make sure that it didn’t go make some low-level change to [your] low-level security, didn’t make an outbound network call, didn’t try to open a file that it shouldn’t.”

Google is also working with Anyscale Inc. on KubeRay, which runs Anyscale’s Ray platform natively on Kubernetes so platform teams can offer distributed training and inference to many research groups, Singh noted. OpenRL brings that approach to reinforcement learning, which teaches post-trained models guardrails, Naim added.

“In the past, to do reinforcement learning, you needed to hire a dozen research scientists with PhDs,” Naim said. “Our goal was, ‘How can we bring reinforcement learning into the world of platform engineering so that you can run reinforcement learning on your Kubernetes environment and take advantage of it to actually do continuous improvement for your agentic workload?'”

Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA:

#5449. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5448. Mortgage industry expects CFPB servicing rule to narrow

The CFPB has sent a revised version of its 2024 “Streamlining Mortgage Servicing for Borrowers Experiencing Payment Difficulties” rule to the Office of Management and Budget, moving closer to finalizing new loss-mitigation standards under Regulation X. Industry attorneys expect a significantly narrower rule than the original proposal, shaped by President Trump’s directive to modernize Dodd-Frank-era rules and broad stakeholder pushback against open-ended requirements.  AI Summary

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) last week took another step toward finalizing new loss-mitigation standards, sending a revised version of its 2024 mortgage servicing proposal to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review.

The final rule, “Streamlining Mortgage Servicing for Borrowers Experiencing Payment Difficulties” under Regulation X, is expected to be narrower than the 2024 proposal advanced when the CFPB was led by Rohit Chopra, according to industry attorneys. The CFPB did not immediately reply to HousingWire‘s request for comments.

The move comes in the wake of President Donald Trump’s March 13 executive order, “Promoting Access to Mortgage Credit,” which directs the CFPB to modernize Dodd-Frank-era rules that lenders and servicers say increase compliance costs. The current standards were finalized in 2013.

“We won’t know the final rule’s content until it is published. But the comment record and the current Bureau’s priorities point toward a significantly narrower rule,”Joseph M. DeFazio and Joe Reilly, partners at Troutman Pepper Locke, wrote in a blog post. “Since President Trump’s second term began, the Bureau has also rescinded prior guidance and signaled that it prefers clear, fixed rules to open-ended frameworks like the one in the 2024 proposal.”

The CFPB received more than 80 comments on the proposal, with what the attorneys described as an “unusual degree of convergence” among groups that rarely agree.

The American Bankers Association (ABA) has urged the CFPB to finalize only a limited portion of the 2024 proposal, pressing the bureau to focus on targeted changes rather than a full rewrite.

“The Bureau’s 2024 proposal was founded on the misconception that servicers prioritize foreclosure over helping borrowers find a successful solution to resolve their payment disruptions,” Teshale Smith, the ABA’s senior counsel for regulatory compliance and policy, said in a letter to the CFPB in June. “In fact, sustained low foreclosure rates and high customer satisfaction rates demonstrate that servicers remain committed to helping struggling borrowers.”

The 2024 proposed rule aimed to make permanent several pandemic-era practices used when large numbers of borrowers needed fast assistance. Industry estimates showed that 8.8 million families were helped, with the re-default rate for loans exiting COVID-19 loss-mitigation programs at about 10%, ABA said in its letter.The proposal allows servicers to evaluate loss-mitigation options before borrowers complete an application, prohibits late fees and other charges while a loss-mitigation review is underway, and makes assistance possible in multiple languages.As it relates to foreclosure, the draft allows a loss-mitigation review cycle to start when the borrower asks for help, not only after a completed application, lasting until the loan is current or all options are ruled out. During that time, servicers could not begin or advance foreclosure, a protection that currently applies only after a complete application is on file. Foreclosure could resume only after options were exhausted or the borrower stopped communicating.

Attorneys at Troutman Pepper Locke expect the final rule to permit sequential review of loss-mitigation options instead of requiring servicers to evaluate all options at once; dropping the proposed ban on fee accrual during loss-mitigation reviews; and removal of the language access provisions that were part of the 2024 draft.

Isaac Boltansky, head of public policy at Pennymac, said the company “supports clear, consistent standards that give servicers the certainty they need to deliver the best possible outcomes for homeowners, particularly those facing financial hardship.”

#5446. Agents idling while they wait on humans push Kubernetes to hand back unused resources

Agentic AI workloads are handing Kubernetes an unexpected second act. The orchestrator once dismissed as reliable but boring is now at the center of how enterprises plan to run autonomous software.

Past platform shifts, from physical servers to virtual machines and from virtual machines to containers, forced companies to wipe the slate clean and start over. This shift is different because Kubernetes was built as a platform for building platforms, according to Bobby Allen (pictured), cloud therapist at Google Cloud LLC.

“Kubernetes now, 11, 12+ years in, has this whole new life,” Allen said. “You don’t need a new platform this time. … This shift doesn’t mean that you’ve got to retool and rebuild and replatform everything, and I think that could be comforting for folks to realize that they don’t have to start from scratch.”

Allen spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Kubernetes is recovering resources spent on idle agentic AI workloads. (* Disclosure below.)

Google is putting that view into practice. The company has donated Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, while engineering teams are tuning Kubernetes for agents rather than building a new stack.

“Google is doubling down on our commitment to not just open source but community-driven, collaborative, multiple-partner-involvement open source,” Allen said. “These concepts are foundational, but they’re important enough that we need to all contribute and shape these together.”

Efficiency is a big part of the motivation. Agents spend long stretches idle while they wait for human input, and the projects aim to give those resources back during the downtime, Allen explained.

“These are kind of different efforts that contribute to an open, flexible, transparent, collaborative way to make agentic workloads run better so that we can have these amazing outcomes but also be efficient with our resources,” Allen said. “We don’t want to have this sci-fi Star Trek moment where we’re stepping into the future and kill the planet.”

#5445. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

#5444. Builder credit conditions tighten for 19th straight quarter

NAHB’s Q3 2026 AD&C Financing survey shows credit for land acquisition, development and construction tightened for the 19th consecutive quarter, mirroring Federal Reserve loan officer data. Contract rates moved only modestly and were offset by lower points, keeping effective borrowing costs elevated across most AD&C categories. Builders are increasingly using construction-to-permanent loans tied to end buyers, with 32% of respondents using them and, for those, 58% of homes financed this way. Persistent tight AD&C lending threatens to slow lot development and new-home supply, reinforcing structural housing shortages even as the mortgage market shows its own signs of stress.  AI Summary

Credit conditions for residential land acquisition, development and construction (AD&C) loans tightened again in the third quarter of 2026, extending a nearly five-year stretch of more restrictive lending for homebuilders, according to a National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) survey.

NAHB’s quarterly AD&C Financing survey showed a net easing index of -15.3 in Q3, meaning more builders and developers reported tighter credit than easier credit. It marks the 19th consecutive quarter of net tightening for AD&C borrowers, NAHB economist Paul Emrath wrote in an analysis published Nov. 13.

The findings closely track the Federal Reserve’s October survey of senior loan officers. NAHB reported that the Fed’s net easing index for residential AD&C loans came in at -15.5 in the third quarter. Aside from modest lender-reported easing in the second quarter of 2026, both lenders and builders have indicated that AD&C credit has been tightening steadily since early 2022. The Fed’s index has been in negative territory in 18 of the past 19 quarters.

For homebuilders and land developers, those readings underscore that bank appetite for risk in residential construction remains weak even as broader housing demand depends on new supply.

While credit availability continued to contract, AD&C financing costs showed only modest quarter-to-quarter movement in the third quarter, with no clear trend toward either higher or lower overall borrowing costs.

NAHB reported the following changes in average contract interest rates between the second and third quarters of 2026:

At the same time, initial points on AD&C loans declined across all four categories, NAHB found:

Those offsetting moves left effective borrowing costs — which combine contract rates and points — little changed for most types of AD&C credit:

For builders, the message is that even where nominal rates tick lower, the all-in cost of capital for lots and vertical construction remains high by historical standards. Combined with tighter underwriting, that environment can slow lot pipeline development, constrain spec building and push more risk and cost back onto builders’ balance sheets.

NAHB’s third-quarter survey also highlighted increased use of construction-to-permanent, or one-time-close, loans tied directly to the end buyer.

Among survey respondents who built single-family homes in the third quarter, 32% said they financed at least some production with construction-to-permanent loans to the ultimate homebuyer. On average, 58% of the homes those respondents built were financed this way, NAHB reported.

Those structures can help builders reduce their direct exposure to AD&C credit by shifting some financing to retail mortgage channels earlier in the process. They can also appeal to buyers looking to lock both construction and permanent financing terms in a single transaction, an important hedge in a volatile rate environment.

NAHB noted that market stress in residential mortgages – including a recent drop in applications and rising delinquencies – has drawn significant attention. But the group argued that constrained AD&C financing is an underappreciated bottleneck for adding new supply, especially in affordable and entry-level segments.

Because AD&C loans finance land pipelines, infrastructure and vertical construction, persistently tight lending standards can limit lot development, delay projects and reduce the number of homes that reach the for-sale market. That dynamic can amplify the impact of low existing-home inventory and keep upward pressure on home prices and rents.

For builders, developers and their lenders, the survey results suggest that planning assumptions for 2027 should continue to factor in restricted credit availability, elevated effective borrowing costs and a need for diversified capital sources, including joint ventures, private capital and greater use of buyer-based construction-to-perm structures.

More detail on credit conditions for residential builders and developers, including cross-tabs on lender behavior and loan terms, is available on NAHB’s AD&C Financing Survey web page.

#5442. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure shakes AI industry’s foundations

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

Honeypot or not, the Chinese executive/accused spy with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted an affair this week should have been a flashing red light to him. So should fraternizing with one of your own VPs — and reportedly another employee too!

In the end, all that, and maybe more to come, was just too much for Nvidia’s board to bear despite the commanding position Huang (pictured) held not only at Nvidia but in the entire artificial intelligence industry. Indeed, the speed with which he resigned — spectacularly stupid as his behavior was — still makes me wonder if there are other shoes to drop, especially on the legal or national security fronts. Market researcher SemiAnalysis thinks it came down to pressure from the U.S. intelligence community that’s very unhappy Nvidia chips have apparently been smuggled to China.

Huang was something of an AI puppet master, providing the chips and software to power the entire industry as well as seemingly unlimited cash to fund and backstop everyone from AI leaders such as OpenAI and Anthropic to innumerable cloud compute providers worldwide. No single person inside or outside Nvidia seems likely to fill that role.

However, Nvidia really is much more than Jensen Huang. Interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress helped craft the financial arrangements that in part put Nvidia at the center of AI — though for what it’s worth, Huang himself wasn’t a fan lately. Some of his direct reports such as high-performance computing chief Ian Buck seem quite capable of carrying on, if perhaps not with Huang’s panache. One company is never one person, and shouldn’t be. I expect a less centralized Nvidia going forward, whoever’s at the top.

More than that, AI is much more than Jensen Huang, and it will continue to be going forward. It’s easy to forget that although Huang brilliantly helped create this new wave, AI and its enablers also are what made him a rock star. But that time is now over. Nvidia and certainly the AI industry shouldn’t be depending on one person to keep everything afloat anyway.

The reverberations of his sudden and shocking departure will continue to echo for a long time to come across Nvidia, its investors watching hundreds of billions of market cap evaporate, legions of Jensen fanboys and the entire artificial intelligence ecosystem. A lot of people are hoping desperately that he didn’t just pop the AI bubble (though others are thinking he did). It seems unlikely this will be the pin, but we’re dealing with a lot of unlikely things in the past week or so, for better and worse, and this shock is clearly rattling the foundations.

All that managed to overshadow what otherwise would be the big news this week: Anthropic went on the road to pitch its initial public offering. It’s hoping to raise more than $64 billion and keep the AI trade humming in Nvidia’s near-term absence. Looks like next Thursday is the big day.

And it’s not the only good news in AI — that is, if the IPO is successful. After a difficult month on the stock front, uber neocloud CoreWeave provided a pleasant AI surprise with upside earnings and guidance, lifting its shares almost 25% Wednesday. AI chipmaker Cerebras’ shares rose almost 18% in late trading Thursday on positive guidance and a Microsoft deal. Cisco Systems said demand is strong for AI infrastructure, even if investors shrugged, and chipmaking equipment supplier Applied Materials said AI boosted demand as well.

Not everyone fared so well, though. Dutch neocloud Nebius saw its shares drop almost 17% Thursday as it lowered its outlook despite close to sevenfold revenue growth in the last quarter. The stock drop no doubt was partly because of Nvidia, which is, of course, an investor. CoreWeave –yes, another Nvidia investment — lost 7% Thursday.

Couple of really big outages out there: first, Microsoft Outlook, grounding a lot of office workers, then the whole damn U.S. air traffic control system, grounding thousands of flights.

Sovereignty is on many enterprise buyers’ lips these days, the notion that enterprises need a way to assert more control over their technology estates and protect their customers’ data. TheCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin just completed the first of a series of reports on how to approach sovereignty, this one focused on the hyperscale cloud providers.

The software orchestrator Kubernetes has become boring, but as SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier said at this week’s KubeCon in Salt Lake City, that means it’s a success — with lessons for AI developers. “A lot of things that are happening in cloud-native that were involved in microservices in Kubernetes world are actually the same challenges in the AI world,” he noted.

IBM has been working hard on quantum computing for a long time now, but at its Quantum Developer Conference in Chicago this week, it showed significant progress, according to Dave Vellante. Its goal now is to show actual industry impact by 2028, a laudable goal that presents a lot of challenges, Dave wrote in his Special Breaking Analysis this week.

Next week the SC26 high-performance computing conference comes to Chicago, and theCUBE and theCUBE Research will be onsite with interviews and analysis. There’s also Microsoft Ignite in San Francisco. And earnings next week include… Nvidia! Bring the popcorn.

Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, most of it not salacious, along with analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:

Breaking Analysis: Sovereign or not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide

Breaking Analysis: AI cyber resilience and the trust gap

Dario goes overboard with AI claims ahead of Anthropic’s IPO — the same guy who says AI could also extinguish us. Somebody give him back his Xanax! Also, I really don’t think mental illness is a compute problem.

Gartner forecasts AI infrastructure spending to represent 59% of total global AI spending in 2027

Gartner also forecasts AI will drive a net increase of 1.7M jobs by 2030 That one number hides a lot of job losses and especially job “transformations,” and not to throw shade on Gartner in particular, anyone betting on AI’s impact out in 2030 is barely more than guessing.

United Airlines is banning AI bots from booking flights, following Amazon and Walmart doing the same thing for shopping. Aren’t travel and shopping a prime use case for AI agents? But they’re still trying: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its ‘dots’ AI agents to make purchases for users.

Getting too close to Trump was a mistake, says Nick Clegg. Amen. We’ve already seen them trying to backpedal, starting with Palantir CEO Alex Karp, who had the audacity to call his company “progressive.” Dude, sit down.

#5441. Why Midwest buyer demand is holding up in the face of higher mortgage rates

Midwest metros, including Columbus and Cincinnati, are keeping pending sales near or above new listings as mortgage activity stays mixed. Lower list prices and smaller loan amounts appear to support demand, even with rates above 7% pressuring affordability.  AI Summary

Several Midwest housing markets are showing signs of resilient buyer demand compared to other parts of the country, with pending home sales keeping pace with new listings even as purchase mortgage activity remains largely flat or declines.

Columbus, Ohio, had 127 pending sales for every 100 new listings as of Nov. 6, according to HousingWire Data. Cincinnati followed at 125. These markets were well above the national average of 95 pending sales per 100 new listings, while Cleveland (91) and St. Louis (90) were running slightly below the U.S. average.

The same markets also had median list prices that were considerably lower than the national average of $429,000. Cleveland led the way at $174,000, followed by St. Louis ($225,000), Columbus ($255,000) and Cincinnati ($300,000).

In St. Louis, buyers remain active despite elevated mortgage rates, although they are being more deliberate about their decisions, said Greg Iverson, a divisional sales manager for Neighborhood Loans.

“I wouldn’t say it’s necessarily a buyer’s market, but it’s starting to become that way in certain areas,” Iverson said in an interview with HousingWire.

Like most buyers nationwide, affordability remains the biggest obstacle for his clients, Iverson said. Mortgage rates above 7% have added to the rising costs of property taxes, homeowners insurance, building materials and home repairs. Inventory has also increased in some price ranges, he said, but not across the board.

But Iverson said St. Louis continues to see activity from first-time and move-up buyers alike since the market’s lower home prices have helped keep these buyers from being priced out entirely.

A similar pattern is playing out in smaller Ohio markets. Scott Snapp, a Findlay, Ohio-based branch manager at loanDepot, said his business has remained steady, with loan applications coming in at about the same pace as last year.

When comparing his October 2026 production with the same point a year earlier, Snapp said he had closed 57 loans totaling $12 million last year, versus 51 loans totaling $11 million at the time of the interview. Snapp said his average loan size is about $215,000.

“I’m not seeing a drop, realistically,” he said. “Applications coming in are still at the same pace as they were last year around here.”

Mortgage data platform Modex shows that purchase lending has been relatively steady in several Midwest markets, but it has not uniformly increased.

Cleveland was the only one of four Midwest metros in HousingWire’s comparison to record year-over-year growth in purchase loans from January through July, with 11,809 loans, up 0.9%. Cincinnati recorded 14,048 loans, down 2.2%, while Columbus had 12,820, down 2.7%. St. Louis recorded 9,811 loans, a 6.8% decline. The St. Louis figure excludes St. Louis County since 2026 county records were still being updated.

Modex data indicated that median purchase loan amounts in these Midwest markets ranged from $217,075 in Cleveland to $294,566 in Columbus. Lower loan amounts and home prices could attest to some of the Midwest’s relative resilience. More than 20% of purchase loans in Cleveland and St. Louis were for less than $150,000.

But the resilience is still being tested. Jason Harris, a Columbus-based branch manager at Rate, described September as a slow month for contracts that would have closed in October. And he expected October to be one of the slower months the market had seen in years due to higher mortgage rates.

But he added that contract activity improved over the course of October as mortgage rates eased.

“I feel blessed to be in Columbus because it’s still an area where you can purchase an affordable home,” Harris said. “Affordability is something that is so desperately needed by buyers right now. … Even three-eighths of a percent is having a meaningful impact on demand.”

Harris said first-time buyers, as well as borrowers using down payment assistance and state bond programs, typically make up a larger share of his business late in the year. These buyers, coupled with lower-priced homes, typically bring down his average loan size in the fourth quarter, while also driving more Federal Housing Administration loans and government-backed adjustable-rate mortgages, he said.

Back in St. Louis, Iverson said the metro area has continued to attract interest from real estate investors, including those who are becoming more selective about where they purchase as costs rise in other markets.

Snapp also pointed to local employment as a source of housing demand in his part of Ohio, citing new distribution centers and business activity, including facilities opened by Amazon and planned by Sheetz.

“We’re seeing a lot of businesses coming into this area and opening up, and that’s helped us,” he said.

The market has also benefited from buyers relocating from other states, Snapp said. Some have moved for work, while others are returning to the area to be near family.

St. Louis and smaller Ohio markets contrast with areas where mortgage professionals have reported weaker activity. Iverson said he has heard of homes sitting longer in markets such as San Diego, while Snapp said colleagues in Las Vegas and Seattle had described slower conditions.

Harris said he expects demand in central Ohio to pick up again as the market moves into 2027, even if some buyers are postponing purchases until the spring. He said the region’s underlying need for housing remains strong.

“The number of people that need homes and want homes in central Ohio over the next five years is going to be good,” he said.
